narrative.headline: Florida payroll employment is higher than a year ago; unemployment is 4.6%.
whatStandsOut: Nonfarm Payrolls are up 41.0k over the last year.
Labor Force is up 44,356 people year-over-year.
improving: The unemployment rate is 4.6%, up 0.7 percentage points over the year.
Private Education & Health Services is among the strongest job growers (2.2% YoY).
Leisure & Hospitality is among the strongest job growers (1.0% YoY).
Manufacturing is among the strongest job growers (1.0% YoY).
whyItMatters: Payroll jobs and employed residents are different measures. Their trends should be assessed separately.
Industry-level changes show where hiring is expanding or contracting within the statewide total.
Population changes affect demand for housing, services, and infrastructure, but do not by themselves establish business investment or productivity growth.

narrative.headline: Business applications, sector employment, and output measure different aspects of Florida's economy.
signals: Professional & business services employment is up 0.8% year-over-year.
development: Real gross state product is up 11.9% over three years.
momentum: Business applications measure filings rather than operating firms or jobs created.
Information and professional-services employment cover broad industries and are not direct measures of AI activity.
Investment decisions also require local evidence on talent, infrastructure, and project delivery.

clusters.title: AI capex and power readiness
clusters.thesis: Florida's AI infrastructure position requires comparable evidence on data-center capacity, power availability, project investment, and employment.
clusters.bottleneck: Power supply, water, transmission, and the allocation of infrastructure costs.
clusters.proof: State unemployment rates alone cannot establish whether Florida is gaining or losing AI infrastructure investment.
clusters.whatToTrack: Data-center megawatts, interconnection queue, industrial power rates, project capex, and high-wage construction plus operations jobs.

clusters.title: Space Coast aerospace cadence
clusters.thesis: Florida's aerospace capabilities connect launch operations, manufacturing, engineering, and spaceport infrastructure.
clusters.bottleneck: Specialized talent, industrial sites, supplier depth, and how much of the value chain stays in Florida.
clusters.proof: Space Florida's 2025 review reported 109 launches and a $6 billion prospective project pipeline. The $600 million Blue Origin expansion was announced in May 2026.
clusters.whatToTrack: Launch cadence, aerospace payrolls, project pipeline, supplier announcements, and advanced manufacturing wage growth.

clusters.title: LATAM gateway and logistics
clusters.thesis: South Florida's trade capabilities connect ports and airports with logistics, finance, and business services.
clusters.bottleneck: Cold-chain capacity, port throughput, customs efficiency, insurance, and last-mile infrastructure.
clusters.proof: PortMiami and Port Everglades publish cargo statistics that provide dated measures of regional freight activity.
clusters.whatToTrack: TEUs, tonnage, refrigerated cargo, LATAM share, air cargo, export categories, and bilateral trade via Florida ports and airports.

clusters.title: Talent pipeline and wage outcomes
clusters.thesis: Industry development depends on education, skills, and employer demand aligning across Florida's regional labor markets.
clusters.bottleneck: The first Talent Match view covers selected public-university bachelor's pathways; state-college, private, certificate, graduate, migration, and employer-demand layers remain outside the proxy.
clusters.proof: The selected pathways combine historical graduate outcomes with long-term occupational projections. They are incomplete measures of labor supply and demand.
clusters.whatToTrack: Broader credentials, regional placement, retention, target occupations, wage outcomes, and employer demand in priority clusters.

scenarios.label: Base case
scenarios.summary: Florida keeps gaining people, income, and company formation, but high-wage cluster depth grows unevenly.
signals: Labor force keeps expanding while unemployment stays elevated from recent lows.
Business applications increase while information-sector employment follows a different trend.
Trade and aerospace carry distinctive strength, but AI infrastructure remains under-measured.

scenarios.label: Ambition case
scenarios.summary: Illustrative scenario: additional investment in AI, aerospace, logistics, life sciences, and business services, with project-specific infrastructure costs covered.
signals: Data-center and grid investments show up as high-wage construction and operations jobs.
Space Coast suppliers deepen the aerospace value chain inside Florida.
Talent pipeline data begins showing cluster-specific wage and placement gains.

scenarios.label: Risk case
scenarios.summary: Florida keeps the migration story but misses too much of the power-heavy capex and STEM employment boom.
signals: Unemployment rises while payroll growth concentrates in lower-wage or population-serving sectors.
Texas, Georgia, Arizona, and North Carolina absorb more industrial and data-center investment.
Employment and wage gains fall short of the state's industry-development ambitions.

forecasts.claim: Research question: how much AI infrastructure investment is Florida attracting relative to comparable states?
forecasts.mechanism: Data-center projects may generate construction, engineering, utility, and operating activity. Their contribution must be established from project-level capacity, spending, employment, and cost data.
leadingIndicators: Announced megawatts and MW under construction by state
Large-load interconnection queue and utility tariff filings
Hyperscaler, neocloud, and colocation capex announcements
laggingIndicators: Average weekly wages in target clusters
forecasts.baseCase: Illustrative scenario: established industries continue to account for most documented regional investment.
forecasts.ambitionCase: Illustrative scenario: commercially viable compute projects add capacity while covering their infrastructure costs and supporting regional demand.
forecasts.riskCase: Illustrative scenario: infrastructure constraints delay viable projects or increase their costs.
forecasts.counterCase: Labor-market changes may reflect participation, industry composition, and broader conditions rather than AI investment.
forecasts.updateTrigger: Reassess when comparable project-capacity inventories and utility filings are available. No causal finding is established here.

forecasts.claim: Research question: which Florida economic-development practices are transferable to other regions?
forecasts.mechanism: Policy comparisons require evidence on institutions, costs, industry composition, and outcomes. Florida's geographic and demographic advantages may not transfer.
forecasts.baseCase: Illustrative scenario: evidence supports selected practices under comparable local conditions.
forecasts.ambitionCase: Illustrative scenario: documented improvements in investment delivery and workforce outcomes inform other jurisdictions.
forecasts.riskCase: Policies are adopted without accounting for differences in local conditions or implementation capacity.
forecasts.counterCase: Geography, climate, migration, and industry structure may explain outcomes that are incorrectly attributed to policy.
forecasts.updateTrigger: Reassess after comparable outcome studies become available.

policyMemos.title: Data-center investment and infrastructure costs.
policyMemos.stance: Editorial recommendation: assess viable data-center investment alongside ratepayer protection and local infrastructure requirements.
policyMemos.whatChanged: CS/CS/SB 484 became Chapter 2026-65. Its principal effective date is July 1, 2026, with exceptions identified in the law.
policyMemos.mechanism: Project evaluation should distinguish private investment benefits from electricity, water, and infrastructure costs borne by other customers.
policyMemos.recommendation: Assess power procurement, water use, grid requirements, cost recovery, and employment commitments for each proposal. Any incentives should have explicit terms and measurable public benefits.
policyMemos.whatNotToDo: Do not infer public benefits from announced spending alone or assume all data centers have the same costs and operating requirements.
nextMoves: Add Florida-specific MW pipeline and utility tariff tracker
Create a named project ledger for data centers, grid upgrades, and advanced manufacturing
Map strategic workloads to Space Coast, LATAM, health, finance, and emergency-resilience use cases

policyMemos.title: Make wage quality the referee.
policyMemos.stance: Editorial recommendation: evaluate industry policy using wages, productivity, and sustained employment alongside investment totals.
policyMemos.whatChanged: The latest employment figures differ by industry and measure. Aggregate growth does not establish the quality of individual jobs.
policyMemos.mechanism: Population affects demand. Capital investment can support productive capacity, but outcomes depend on project type, implementation, and workforce capabilities.
policyMemos.recommendation: Use occupational wages, QCEW industry data, credentials, and regional employment outcomes to assess progress.
policyMemos.whatNotToDo: Do not substitute business applications, migration-related income, or announced jobs for measured wage outcomes.
nextMoves: Add high-wage occupation basket by cluster
Track target-cluster wages versus state median
Connect education programs and credentials to employment outcomes

projectLedger.headline: The announcement is the start. Conversion is the score.
projectLedger.summary: A source-backed ledger of named strategic projects in Florida and competitor states, normalized so executives can compare disclosed capital, jobs, timing, and delivery stage without double-counting headline packages.
projectLedger.coverageNote: Curated strategic-project coverage, not a complete census of statewide business investment. Totals include only disclosed capital tied to named facilities. Peer projects span four states and are not aggregated as a state-to-state ranking.
methodology: Count disclosed investment only when it is tied to a named facility or expansion.
Exclude contracts, purchase orders, grants, aggregate pipelines, and public-program totals from project capex.
Treat announced and site-selected projects as pipeline; count only construction and operating stages as converted.
Count direct announced jobs in job totals; positions merely supported or retained remain visible but are excluded.

governmentGrantsLedger.headline: Public capital is only useful when it builds strategic capacity.
governmentGrantsLedger.summary: A decision ledger of named government grant and cooperative-agreement awards in Florida and competitor states, normalized by funding source, recipient, delivery status, and documented economic leverage.
governmentGrantsLedger.coverageNote: Curated strategic-award coverage from 2024 through 2026, not a complete accounting of government assistance. Totals include only official named awards. Appropriations, open opportunities, contracts, and multi-award program headlines remain visible as context but are never added to award totals.
methodology: Count an item only after an official source names the recipient and award amount.
Separate the government source of funds from the agency administering a pass-through award.
Exclude appropriations, application cycles, procurement contracts, loans, tax incentives, and aggregate program capacity from award totals.
Use current obligations for active federal awards when available; do not count a possible multi-year ceiling as money awarded.
Count documented private or non-award capital as leverage only when an official award announcement provides the amount.

awards.strategicRead: This is Florida's largest recent named strategic workforce award, but success depends on employer uptake, apprenticeship completions, wage gains, and conversion into production capacity rather than the headline alone.

awards.stageDetail: Road and workforce-housing infrastructure is intended to support industrial development near the Port of Port St. Joe.
awards.strategicRead: The award addresses enabling infrastructure around an industrial site, but the named private project and follow-on capital remain the evidence gap.

awards.recipient: Gulf County Board of County Commissioners
awards.stageDetail: Award supports a self-docking floating dry dock and mooring infrastructure at Eastern Shipbuilding Group.
awards.strategicRead: This is the most direct current example of Florida using public infrastructure capital to deepen shipbuilding capacity, though it is far smaller than the permanent sector tools deployed by leading peers.

awards.stageDetail: Award supports a commercial driver's license training facility serving North Central Florida.
awards.strategicRead: Useful workforce capacity, but an executive scorecard should test completions, employer placement, wages, and whether the training supports strategic logistics and industrial projects.

awards.recipient: Nassau County Board of County Commissioners
awards.stageDetail: More than $6 million supports a roadway network serving an industrial and commercial development site.
awards.strategicRead: The grant creates site readiness, but the ledger should not infer private investment or jobs until a named company commitment is verified.

awards.program: CDBG-Disaster Recovery Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Match
awards.stageDetail: Disaster-recovery funds support a public-safety safe room and generators for critical facilities.

awards.fundingAgency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
awards.program: CDBG-Disaster Recovery Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Match
awards.stageDetail: Disaster-recovery funds support generators for critical public facilities.
awards.strategicRead: This is defensive infrastructure capital: economically necessary, but not evidence of new strategic-industry investment.

awards.fundingAgency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
awards.program: CDBG-Disaster Recovery Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Match
awards.stageDetail: Disaster-recovery funds support emergency generators at school facilities.
awards.strategicRead: The award strengthens continuity and shelter capacity; it should not be presented as a business-investment win.

awards.stageDetail: TSIF grant supports Samsung's advanced semiconductor manufacturing expansion in Taylor.
awards.strategicRead: One Texas sector-specific award is more than twice the disclosed total of the Florida awards in this curated ledger and is tied to $4.73 billion of company investment.

awards.stageDetail: TSIF grant supports a semiconductor materials expansion with more than $154 million in capital investment.
awards.strategicRead: Texas is using a repeatable specialist fund to compound an existing semiconductor cluster, not waiting for a general-purpose economic development program to fit the project.

awards.stageDetail: TSIF grant supports an Austin expansion with more than $71 million in capital investment and more than 320 new jobs.
awards.strategicRead: The grant combines design talent, company capital, and a named jobs commitment, showing that sector tools can target both fabrication and the higher-value semiconductor stack.

awards.stageDetail: TSIF grant supports a semiconductor equipment and services expansion with more than $25 million in capital investment.
awards.strategicRead: Texas is filling supplier-chain gaps with smaller awards as well as anchoring megaprojects, an important model for cluster depth.

awards.stageDetail: TSIF grant supports accelerated semiconductor technician training.
awards.strategicRead: The same specialist fund finances both company projects and the talent system, creating a coordinated portfolio rather than disconnected awards.

talent.headline: Florida's education and workforce pathways.
talent.summary: Selected public-university bachelor's programs, observed graduate outcomes, and long-term occupational projections. The report periods are historical benchmarks, not current hiring estimates.
talent.coverageNote: The selected programs exclude state-college, private, certificate, graduate, migration, and adjacent-occupation supply. Graduate-to-opening ratios describe limited coverage, not a labor shortage or surplus. Florida employment matches exclude some employment outside the covered administrative records and cannot establish total employment or retention.
methodology: Demand uses Florida 2022-32 long-term occupational projections published through O*NET OnLine from Projections Central; openings include growth and replacement.
FETPIP's 2023-24 university graduate report remained the latest posted on September 10, 2026. Employment percentages refer to matches in covered Florida records, not all employment.
The coverage proxy divides covered bachelor's graduates by projected annual openings. It sizes a visible pipeline; it does not label a shortage or surplus.
Institution leaders are the three largest disclosed producers in the selected FETPIP program; suppressed values remain unavailable.
Project pressure links only to named records in the Floridanomics project capex ledger and is not a complete hiring forecast.
